See Abu al-Faraj al-Isfahani, The Book of Songs (al-Aghani), vol. 8, p. 92. ↩

Al-Tabari, vol. 7, p. 26. Khalid's rule was marked by violence and cruelty. Al-Tabari even said of him that “he showed such favouritism that he corrupted the people”. During his long governorship (105–120 AH), he devoted himself to humiliating the religious movements opposed to the Umayyads and amassing vast fortunes. Because his mother was a Christian, Christians enjoyed privileges under his rule that many Muslims did not. One poet, condemning his rule and welcoming his successor in Iraq, Yusuf ibn Umar, said:
He came to us when the polytheists were collecting our alms, And judging us in what we kept hidden and what we made known.
See al-Tabari, vol. 7, p. 47; al-Dimashqi, p. 28. ↩
Wellhausen, The Arab State, p. 352. Nothing shows more clearly how al-Walid ibn Yazid drew inspiration from the ideas of the Mu'tazilites and the Murji'ites than his address on coming to power:

... You will receive your allowances from me each year and your provisions each month, so that Muslims will enjoy the same standard of living, those farthest away as much as those nearest. If I fulfil what I have promised, you must listen to me, obey me and give me your full support. But if I fail to keep my promises, you may remove me and call on me to repent. If I repent, accept my repentance. If you know of any upright man who is willing to give you the same assurances I have given you, and you wish to pledge allegiance to him, I will be the first to do so and obey him. People, no created being is owed obedience when that means disobeying the Creator, nor is loyalty owed to one who breaks his promise. Obedience is owed to God. Obey your ruler in obedience to God as long as he obeys Him. If he disobeys God and calls on you to do the same, he deserves to be disobeyed. I say these words and ask God to forgive both me and you.
History of the Arab State, p. 358. ↩

One of their advocates, Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman, is said to have gone to Basra to spread Murji'ite beliefs secretly. He took up residence in its mosque under the guise of teaching children. When his purpose became known, the students refused to learn from him, so he left the city in a hurry. See al-Dhahabi, vol. 1, p. 596; Ibn Hajar, 3–17 [citation as printed]. ↩
Ibn Hazm, The Distinction Between Religions, Doctrines and Sects (Al-Fasl fi al-Milal wa al-Ahwa wa al-Nihal), vol. 4, p. 204. ↩
Same work and page; Van Vloten, Arab Supremacy, Shiism and Israelite Traditions, p. 125. ↩

Imam Abu Hanifa also held that the Quran was created and that people had free will. It has even been said that he was a Murji'ite and, like Jahm ibn Safwan, was influenced by the ideas of al-Jad ibn Dirham. Whether Abu Hanifa held Murji'ite beliefs is a question on which scholars, past and present, have disagreed. On this subject, see al-Ashari, The Beliefs of the Muslims, p. 138 and following; al-Khatib al-Baghdadi, History of Baghdad, vol. 13, p. 323 and following; al-Shahrastani, vol. 1, p. 121; Ahmad Amin, The Morning of Islam, vol. 3, p. 322 and following. ↩
History of the Arab State, p. 368. ↩
Forgiveness and tolerance were among the defining features of the Murji'ite movement in Khurasan. They were celebrated even by the poets of the Abbasid age. Abu Nuwas says:
Though I have done wrong and fallen short, I still hope in the gracious forgiveness of God.

Lord, I call on You humbly, as You commanded me. If You turn away my outstretched hand, who then will show me mercy? I have no way to reach You but through hope, Your gracious forgiveness, and the fact that I am a Muslim.
See Ahmad Amin, The Morning of Islam, vol. 3, p. 329. ↩

The Murji'ites had more followers in Khurasan than the Kharijites, because of their tolerant principles. We know that the two schools competed for supporters: “The leaders of the Shurat [Kharijites] and the Murji'ites would meet and debate in Khurasan” (al-Isfahani, The Book of Songs, vol. 14, p. 269). Naturally, the result favoured the Murji'ites. See Wellhausen, The Arab State, p. 473; Hasan Mahmud, The Islamic World in the Abbasid Age, p. 21. ↩
